articles.title: Wolverine on the PS5 goes back to a simpler (and bloodier) style of action game
articles.summary: Marvel’s Wolverine, from Spider-Man developer Insomniac, is a PS5 exclusive that takes a more old-school approach to combat.
articles.body: Marvel’s Wolverine captures just how angry its lead character is. The latest PS5 exclusive from Spider-Man developer Insomniac, Wolverine is a straightforward action game that is at its best when you’re (literally) slicing through enemies or thrust into a sequence pulled from a blockbuster movie, like climbing the fuselage of a plane as it careens toward land or racing a motorcycle across rain-slicked city streets. It’s the kind of game that can really get your heart rate rising, and keeping Logan mad is a key part of the strategy. In many ways, it’s a throwback to straightforward action titles of the past — and it’s a refreshing change of pace in a medium saturated with live-service and open-world games. Though it comes from Insomniac, Wolverine is very different from Spider-Man, which thrust the web-slinger into an open-world version of New York City. Instead, this is a much more linear experience that feels like a combination of two other PlayStation staples: God of War and Uncharted. Rather than follow Wolverine as a member of the X-Men, the story instead has him as an often reluctant member of Team X, a mercenary group with similar pro-mutant aims but a much more violent approach. Instead of heroes like Cyclops and Professor X, Wolvy is joined by more villain-adjacent characters like Sabretooth, Mystique, and Nathaniel Essex, before eventually connecting with Jean Grey. The story pulls Logan and his companions across the globe, but it starts out relatively simple, as they investigate a rash of mutant disappearances connected to a billionaire arms dealer. The most important thing about both Wolverine the character and Wolverine the game is fighting. This is a hairy little dude who loves to scrap, and his mutant powers — healing and sharp claws — make it so that he is very good at it, able to both take a huge amount of damage and dish it out. And the best part of the game is how Wolverine-specific the action is. The combat is fast and violent and forces you to be aggressive. Wolverine can leap huge distances to take out foes and use his claws to both repel attacks and slice at enemies, often with very gruesome results. (At the end of a battle he’s usually coated in blood.) An important part of this is Wolverine’s rage level, which increases the more you fight. As his rage grows, it allows you to do two things: go absolutely berserk and kill a rash of enemies with a single blow, and use your healing power as a sort of extra life in case your health depletes. It’s a clever system that means you can’t sit back and play it safe. Wolverine isn’t chill, and you can’t be either. [Image: That’s the God of War side of Wolverine. The Uncharted side comes in the form of all of the over-the-top set-pieces you’re thrown into. I’ll refrain from detailing some of the best ones for spoiler reasons, but I’ll say that, just like in Uncharted, these moments make it feel like you’re playing out a wild sequence from an action movie. There are chases across the rooftops of Tokyo, massive boss battles against some iconic comic book villains, and scenes where Wolverine is literally being ripped apart as he fights for survival. The flip side is that, because of this setup, Wolverine is also much more restrictive than most of its contemporaries. In some ways this is a good thing; it’s refreshing to play a game that isn’t trying to do everything. But there are still some awkward elements. For instance, much like in Spider-Man, there are lots of collectibles that will reveal new bits of story or unlock new suits for Wolverine to wear. But exploration outside of the main path is extremely dull, so the only reason to track these down is if you have a completionist mindset. It’s also disappointing that Wolverine’s closet of outfits is much less fun than Spider-Man’s, and they often feel out of place with the game’s attempt at a more gritty tone. Making matters worse is that, despite a promising start, the story ends up in a largely forgettable place, with few surprises, particularly if you have an even slight knowledge of the X-Men universe from comics or the animated series. Outside of combat and set-pieces, Wolverine skews generic AAA game; the voice acting, the cutscenes, and even some of the missions feel like standard video game fare, many of which seem out of place. Wolverine is amazing when you’re surrounded by ninjas trying to kill you. But when Logan is in a tux trying to spy on a fancy party? Not so much. All that said, Wolverine’s return to a simpler and smaller style of action — I beat the game in around 13 hours — is still notable, particularly from Sony, which has had a rough few years after placing many ill-fated bets in the live-service space. But much like last year’s Ghost of Yōtei, Wolverine shows that PlayStation is still capable of the single-player blockbusters the platform is best known for. It’s also launching at perhaps the busiest video game release period in recent memory, going up against major titles including Onimusha: Way of the Sword, Control Resonant, Fire Emblem: Fortune’s Weave, Gears of War: E-Day, Silent Hill: Townfall, Star Wars: Zero Company, and, soon enough, The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time and Grand Theft Auto VI. In that company, despite occasionally skewing generic, Wolverine’s bloodthirsty focus on action is something that makes it stand out. Marvel’s Wolverine launches on September 15th on the PS5.

articles.title: Marvel’s Wolverine is Okay, But Stands in the Shadow of Insomniac’s Spider-Man Series — IGN Review
articles.summary: Marvel's Wolverine's slick and satisfying combat wears thin well before its conclusion, so much so that even its strong character work can't quite save it from being anything more than okay.
articles.body:
I’ve just spilled enough blood to fill four Olympic-sized swimming pools. Thousands are now dead thanks to the adamantium claws given to me by Insomniac Games. Marvel’s Wolverine certainly doesn’t skimp when it comes to violence, and gives you plenty of opportunities to enact it with style. But it takes more than blood to get my heart pumping, and it’s in Logan’s surprisingly nuanced tale of self-acceptance that I felt most connected to this latest portrayal of the most famous of the X-Men. That story is tasked with doing most of the heavy lifting here, with the initially slick and satisfying combat wearing thin well before its conclusion, but even that solid character work can’t quite carry the weight it needs to. Marvel’s Wolverine, much like its lead, is built on a firm skeleton, but what’s crafted around it isn’t nearly as strong.

This tale starts a few decades after James “Logan” Howlett first met Nathaniel Essex and was taken into his mutant community, where he quickly became a crucial member of his task force, Team X. Already an experienced hero, it's clear something sinister is at play when we join him here, and Wolverine is soon sent on a mission to investigate scientist Bolivar Trask amidst reports of missing mutants. From there, it hops around the globe, taking Logan to new places rife with danger and old haunts that stir up buried memories. It’s standard superhero fare, with a couple of predictable turns along the way and some genuinely fun moments in its closing hours. It struggles to tell this story effectively through the action within missions, though, instead reserving any real moments of consequence for the cutscenes that bookend them. That makes for an uneven cadence that joltingly stops and starts rather than flows gracefully.

I like this version of Wolverine a lot, as Liam McIntyre’s performance grants Logan a personality to match his trademark blades – a sharp, surprising hidden depth, housed in a bulky, blunt instrument of a body. He delicately balances the shadows of his past with the future of mutantkind, all while managing his Jekyll and Hyde nature, as animal instincts sometimes break through the compassion he strives to show. That emotion comes through not just in his voice, but in how he’s been designed and animated. He moves around social spaces with a hunched back that reflects a vulnerability that clashes with his biological makeup – a physical manifestation of a dark past weighing him down. That’s a microcosm of Insomniac’s detailed rendition of Wolverine, which has instantly become one of my favourite depictions of the character.

But most of all, I like how he bounces off the other cast members. For all of the screaming and bloodshed, it's when things are taken down to a whisper that this campaign tends to shine. I particularly enjoyed reflective moments in a Madripoor bar with Mystique, a snowy cabin rendezvous with Jean Grey, and the tension between Logan and Victor “Sabretooth” Creed. Krizia Bajos in particular is fantastic as Grey, and anchors a lot of the emotional weight of Wolverine’s tale, often preventing it from fully veering into run-of-the-mill comic book storytelling.

It is frustrating, then, that outside of Logan and Jean, few other characters are given room for their own arcs to develop. They have little to do outside of briefly crossing Wolverine to hinder him, or offering him a few words of wisdom from the other side of a bar. Though it is a credit to the writing team that these more tender moments don’t end up sounding completely out of key, especially when contrasted with the heavy-metal violence occurring on screen whenever the claws come out.

Wolverine’s basic attacks are well-honed tools that sink smoothly into flesh and steel alike, with devastating combos delivered through rapid presses of the square and triangle buttons. It’s incredibly responsive action, with the modern staples like dodges, parries, and special attacks to tear through each enemy. It’s not a complex system, though, and is ultimately quite forgiving. A quick press of triangle will make Logan leap to an enemy within range, and the more you stay on the front foot, the quicker your rage bar will fill up, allowing for critical hits to rip through foes with ease and the safety blanket of a revive in your back pocket. His healing factor also means that he’ll regenerate over time while in combat – a smart, and lore-appropriate, decision that means you never have to scramble around arenas in search of health packs.

Again, the animation work is outstanding. It really feels like after years of making sure Spider-Man didn’t let anyone fall to their death, Insomniac has revelled in all the ways Wolverine can end someone’s life. Brutal finishers, from sliced-up limbs to stabs up through jaws, are employed for a variety of gory outcomes. Maybe I should be placed on some sort of watchlist for saying so, but I really couldn’t get enough of them, reveling in each squelchy spine sever and chest-carving cleave. Throw in some slick camerawork and fight choreography when teaming up with the likes of Jean or Sabretooth for tandem kills, and you’ve got an impressive combat flow from an aesthetic perspective.

There's no denying that wielding those claws is slick, punchy, and wonderfully bloody. It's just a shame, then, that halfway through Wolverine's 15-hour string of missions, I felt like I'd had my fill. The fundamentals are solid, but combat needed a stronger sense of progression to sustain that sensation over a game of this length – especially when you’re asked to cut down hundreds of enemies at a near-relentless pace. Yes, there are unlockable skills and special abilities to build into your repertoire, but only a handful, and you'll gain access to them relatively early on.

I enjoyed spinning around like a lemon-tinged tornado slicing up anyone in my path, and booting people off of skyscrapers and cliff edges is a joy that never got old, but those techniques didn’t change my approach to combat in any significant manner. This lack of evolution in Logan's toolset puts the pressure on two other factors in order for the action to remain exciting: enemy variation and encounter design. Only one of those is executed somewhat successfully.

Whether it be Trask's sci-fi forces or the evil ninja followers of The Hand, there's a consistent drip-feed of new enemy types to sink your claws into, even if every fight is ultimately a test of the same reflexes. These vary from sharp-shooting snipers you'll have to scurry your way toward to hard-hitting brutes with cybernetic embellishments. The problem is, although some may require a few more hits to tear apart or demand two parries to stun instead of one, each fight does pretty much feel the same. When multiple enemy waves are comprised of different units, the action can come alive as you learn to prioritise targets to thin out the herd most efficiently. But this balance isn’t found anywhere near consistently enough.

More often than not, missions take the form of a series of corridors opening up into arenas where getting ambushed is a predictable probability. These arenas aren’t constructed in overly interesting ways either, mainly involving a large flat area filled with melee-based grunts and a sprinkle of higher platforms around the edge for ranged troublemakers. Leaping from enemy to enemy and dodging out of the way of projectiles when a red flash appears takes up most of your time, so the locations these battles take place in quickly start to blend together. For the most part, Wolverine wants you to lunge headfirst into the action and bloody those claws, but it makes for a rather one-note dance.

Outside of the action, there’s not too much to shout about, either. Each linear level does contain collectibles, including material caches required to unlock new outfits, which have both deep cuts and surface scratchers alike when it comes to Wolverine’s design history. I particularly enjoy how you can mix and match the over 30 different suits and claws to create your own fantasy Weapon X. Alongside level-up XP for skills, AP is your main resource for progression, unlocking skills that give you a chance to shape a playstyle a little more to your liking – widening parry windows or reducing damage taken, for example. This can be acquired via two methods: collecting whisky bottles and completing nightmare trials.

The former are much like the caches and just require a sharp eye in order to find them, aside from following Wolverine’s keen nose, which is presented as a glowing blue scent line on screen. I never really found the puzzles in the Spider-Man games to be overly complex, but at least they threw a welcome bit of variety into the mix and got my brain cells tingling a little. Here, you simply walk up to optional collectibles and press the triangle button every time. It feels like a missed opportunity to elevate the mundane. Still, I felt compelled to go back through each level to clean them all up, earning a platinum trophy after just 20 hours.

The nightmare trials are a little more interesting, though. They are a mixture of combat and movement challenges that put your skills to the test if you want to achieve the highest scores and, in turn, earn more AP. Of the small selection, I found reasonable enjoyment in the gauntlet variant, which sends waves of enemies your way in a dreamlike world while offering a choice of buffs and nerfs every few rounds. It’s another example of a PlayStation studio adding roguelike elements to a prestige single-player story game, and at least it hasn’t been delivered in the form of DLC this time around. The real reward for completing these trials, though, is memories taken from Logan’s long life that give extra context to the main story. I mostly found myself simply going through the motions while playing through them, but they’re at least a smart way to infuse challenges with bonus narrative nutrients.

Wolverine is built like a brute, a true powerhouse in combat – but he is also agile outside of it, and it’s a shame those skills are never fully put to the test beyond some loose platforming. He’s quick across the ground, though, and charging straight towards turrets hopelessly firing into his deflecting blades is a fun power trip. A blockbuster sheen runs through all of it, and occasionally its cinematic ambitions break out into full-flung sequences full of enthralling action. One chase that took me across the moon-lit rooftops of Tokyo and through its neon-soaked streets is a real spectacle, but while this sort of scripted cinematic affair is thrilling, they come around too infrequently, all boiling down to holding the right trigger to sprint as fireworks go off around you.

A similar thing can be said for its boss fights, of which there are surprisingly few. Most are remarkably similar in design but executed well enough, like an early face-off with Omega Red – a mutant who stalked my nightmares as a young child. It made for some lovely payback as I chipped away at the tentacled terror’s stagger bar via well-timed parries. Similarly, while I won’t spoil anything, the final boss battle is a real spectacle that puts all of your skills to the test. On the other hand, there’s a Sentinel showdown that essentially boils down to whacking a metal arm for 15 minutes, which would feel more at home in a middle-of-the-road 3D platformer than a top-tier action game. It’s the sort of boss battle that should’ve stayed in the early 2000s, where your towering target mostly sits just outside of the arena.

Marvel's Wolverine: Every Costume in the PS5 Game

Logan is a naturally reclusive character. Even when out of his suit, he's on the fringes of society, equally happy in solitude as he is reluctantly searching for a connection with those trying to break his walls down. He’s basically me, but much hairier. It’s a stark contrast to Spider-Man's open world, which lets you interact with its population as both Peter and his web-slinging alter ego, allowing you to develop his character and build a connection to the city. Logan's lodgings don't provide this same nourishment. Insomniac has intentionally made a very different sort of game here, to be fair, with a much more linear structure and less of a focus on exploration in general – but it’s still notable that the change in direction it chose is far less interactive, and as a result, far less interesting.

When the story is told through handsomely sculpted cutscenes, it holds my attention completely, but the smaller areas that glue all those bigger moments together are reduced to meandering through spaces at a walking pace to inspect photo frames and audio logs. They’re largely ponderous sequences that just feel like needless bloat in a not overly long adventure. I can’t help but feel more could’ve been done here in terms of interactivity.

A prime example is an early stretch where you’re tasked with coaxing a young mutant called Leech out of a room. He demands a password from you, which Logan finds by slowly walking around Essex’s manor as he picks up three crayon-scrawled drawings. Rather than asking you to then solve the riddle spread across these doodles yourself, Logan does so of his own accord upon returning to the locked door. There’s no challenge here, no puzzle to solve. It’s like Marvel’s Wolverine only has two speeds: full-throttle bloodshed and introspective calm. An occasional middle ground would’ve been nice to fill out the in-betweens.

There’s no denying each of its globe-spanning locations is beautifully rendered, and when you're not spending time in stretches of brown underground caverns and grey facility hallways, they really feel visually alive. You'll occasionally be let loose to explore the streets, but don't expect open areas full of surprises; these are much more limited spaces restricted to a few blocks. That size reflects the scope of its story, though. Yes, there's a larger threat at play here, but it’s very much a personal Wolverine tale at its core, and I appreciate how restrained Insomniac has been in its approach to the wider X-Men ensemble. It serves the few characters it chooses to hone in on well, never running the risk of bloating the cast. From this perspective, it’s a decent first step into a different side of the Marvel Universe.

articles.title: Pokémon TCG 30th Celebration Reveals New Look at Legendary Illustration Rares
articles.summary: Get a first look at the Legendary Illustration Rares and classic nostalgia reprints debuting in the upcoming Pokémon TCG 30th Celebration set.
articles.body:
The Pokémon Trading Card Game 30th Celebration expansion is nearly here, releasing on September 16, 2026. This is the first time a set has released simultaneously worldwide , with all major regions - including North America, Europe, Japan, Oceania, and Latin America - all getting the set on the same day.

The closer the big day gets, the more Creatures Inc is giving fans brand-new previews of spectacular special illustration rare and illustration rare cards.

Together with the re-introduction of some of their favourite classics from the Classic Collection, and an exciting set of 30 unique cards featuring Pikachu itself, this is shaping up to be a Celebration for the ages. The latest wave of cards has given us a look at a parade of Legendary Pokémon; feast your eyes!

It’s worth noting that the official press release says that the company has “gathered up a lot of Legendary Pokémon”, not “all” Legendary Pokémon. That would explain why Koraidon, Miraidon, Zacian and Zamazenta are missing from this lineup, at least for now, and why regular Mons like Drifloon have found their way in.

It isn't the first time we've seen the trio of birds from Kanto recently! In fact, earlier this week we saw our first look at some beautiful upcoming illustration rares and special illustration rares below, featuring a connected trio of Articuno, Zapdos, and Moltres.

Themed around a day-night cycle, we saw a whole lot of Pokémon soaking up some rays. Alolan Exeggutor is hosting a lively gathering, Morpeko brings a spark of energy, and Salamence ex soars across the clear blue skies, while Sylveon and Fuecoco bask in the sunlight. The stand out for me though has to be that Maushold card - look at those mice go!

As the day becomes night, new Pokémon appear in the moonlight. A spooky Chandelure floats silently over a closed cafe/ Gholdengo shines brightly in the evening light, Scraggy seems tough and determined, and one of my personal favourites so far in this collection, Jirachi, shoots across the sky just as a star does. Toxtricity and Greninja are off somewhere at the party absolutely schmoving.

​I have to say, I’m absolutely blown away by how gorgeous some of these new illustration rares and special art rares—particularly the Moltres and Alolan Exeggutor cards. Although there is some debate within the community around the reprints of the classics in the Classic Collection, as a fan for so long, I still really value the nostalgic reprints, especially for those who didn't get the chance the first time. I know I’m not the only person who once put my base set Charizard through the washing machine 20 years ago.

Now, having another opportunity to collect these original classics means that everyone can own a piece of Pokémon history without having to spend a lot of money. It's actually quite great to see these classics becoming available again—isn’t that what the 30th anniversary is all about, at the end of the day?

There are so many products you can get your hands on for the 30th anniversary. Of course, getting your hands on these products is notoriously difficult. Bot-buying, retail camping, and the fear that secondary market prices will rise above MSRP before regular fans can get their hands on Elite Trainer Boxes or booster bundles have reached an all-time high. In order to deal with this surge in scalping, Amazon has introduced a ticketed, invite-only lottery system for the 30th Celebration Elite Trainer Boxes and has put them on a "Request an Invite" queue in order to help genuine buyers secure the items close to retail price rather than losing out immediately to automated checkout bots.

Remember that the Pokémon TCG: 30th Celebration expansion will be released on September 16, 2026. Each booster pack contains five foil cards, one foil Basic Energy, and guarantees a one-of-thirty unique Pikachu variant in every pack. Each Pikachu is illustrated by a different artist, with the first designed by the original Pokémon artist, Ken Sugimori, who recreated his Pikachu artwork from Jungle. Will you be catching em all in this milestone celebration?

Sara Heritage is a freelance journalist for IGN, specialising in Pokémon TCG. When she's not gaming, you’ll probably find her building yet another LEGO set she absolutely did not need, or chaining ranked matches in Pokémon Champions.

articles.title: Wolverine Review, Gameplay Impressions, Videos and Top Features
articles.summary: Marvel's Wolverine from developer Insomniac Games couldn't have more hype behind it.
articles.body:
Marvel's Wolverine from developer Insomniac Games couldn't have more hype behind it.

The action-adventure romp, after all, features one of the most recognizable characters on the planet. It's backed by the studio that put out a wave of excellent Spider-Man video games and happens to share that same universe, too.

Granted, Wolverine isn't Spider-Man, which creates some obvious questions around keeping gameplay fresh. The darker, grittier combat and character equate to pretty big tonal shifts for the story and familiarity of the tale, too.

But given Insomniac Games' history, there's no question Wolverine will land as one of the best releases of the year. Longevity and future sequels, then, might be the big question floating around the release at launch.

A Wolverine game can't be anything but grisly, bloody, vulgar and sometimes off-putting.

Insomniac's trio of Spider-Man games were genre-leaders in graphical horsepower and immersion. The detail was sometimes a bit lacking, but given the sheer scale of the open world there, the achievements were staggering.

Same vibes here. This isn't a game with a massive cityscape, but darting through the fictional Madripoor, romping through sewers and other various places all have that attention to detail and fidelity that is simply fantastic.

Same story for the sound design, which boasts the fantastic guttural roars and voice acting the property deserves. And the damage and wear and tear on Logan and his consistently bloody, falling-apart enemies is a little wince-inducing at times, in a good way.

On the gameplay front…this is very much what everyone always thought a top-tier Wolverine game should feel like.

Good, because the power fantasy is there. Wolverine loops in punches and kicks and the environment and combos while popping holes in anyone that gets in his way. Big boss setpieces? Indeed.

But that's also just, well, it. The Spider-Man comparisons are inevitable. The characters are just too different. Peter Parker is a genius who experiments with all types of gadgets, can stick to any surface and gets super acrobatic in his combat. The sheer variety and number of ways to approach any situation was quietly a really big reason for that series of games' successes.

Wolverine has claws and not a lot of patience for any of the other nonsense.

In a video game lens, that means things can get repetitive fast.

Wolverine has combos. He has a leap to close the gap and players will be doing a lot of kicking to break an opponent's blocking stance. He also needs to parry constantly with proper timing to counter very aggressive enemies throughout the game.

Aggression is the name of the game, as expected. Logan has a few special moves to use and, of course, a rage meter. Build this up and players get rewarded with bonus damage on combos and even activate a "last stand" mechanic, a nod to his regenerative healing factor. Fall out of combat for too long, though, and the rage meter starts to diminish.

Not that there aren't some variations. The always-controversial inhibitors are in the game and, at times, remove some of Wolverine's abilities. Like other superhumans, he has enhanced senses too, so he can go the stealth route while tracking baddies.

Make no mistake, this is fun. It just feels right, too. That's important. But Wolverine as a character flies far closer to the sun in terms of general action-adventure third-person combat than Spider-Man, and it shows.

Thankfully, as comic book readers can attest, this isn't the standard Wolverine tale within the scope of the X-Men.

Rather, it's a deep-dive interpretation of his origins and those near his orbit in the early days. In this canon, Logan has left Nathaniel Essex's super team of mutants in recent years, only to rejoin when Bolivar Trask and his Reavers militia start disappearing his fellow mutants.

Side characters include, but certainly aren't limited to notables like Sabretooth, Jean Grey and Mystique. The presentation plays with really fun themes, going super-quiet at times compared to the bombast of the levels and combat. It's easy to get invested and memorable.

Still, the confines of the experience matter. New York and all of its personality and NPCs were a big part of the Spider-Man experience. Seeing the massive world react to him from street level on up, was a big part. Wolverine is much more subdued, demanding even more from the supporting cast, which it mostly gets in a good way.

The overarching narrative isn't going to shock anyone familiar with these types of games. It's solid. Where it really shines, though, is in the careful attention to Logan as a character. He's human when he can be, but filled with distrust, aggression and so much more. A few side items like Nightmare Doors really explore the depth of this character, too, very much in a good way.

Progression-wise, Wolverine hits on the usual notes too. There are meaningful skill trees to invest in and other upgrades that can freshen up the experience a bit.

This isn't an open-world romp, but as a superhero video game, there are little easter egg nods and goodies to collect. Linear levels or not, paying close attention and even getting distracted exploring is a must.

It's all a pretty strong technical feat, too, as Wolverine runs well performance-wise and comes with a robust suite of options, including accessibility must-haves.

Wolverine plays in a much more restrictive sandbox than Spider-Man and it shows in its linearity and combat.

This is essentially what everyone has dreamed about for 30ish years when envisioning a powerhouse Wolverine game. The comic-accurate short guy with the claws is violent, loves hard and goes through a lot in about as gruesome a fashion as possible.

Wolverine is not a God of War or similar experience. It's unabashedly itself and a must-feel experience for those with even a passing shred of interest in the character, or of video games in general.

articles.title: Call of Duty Anti-Cheat Boss Reveals Why Activision Shadow Bans Players Suspected of Cheating Instead of Immediately Permanently Banning Them
articles.summary: The senior director of Call of Duty's anti-cheat system has explained why Activision shadow bans players instead of outright permanently banning them from the game.
articles.body:
The senior director of Call of Duty's anti-cheat system has explained why Activision shadow bans players instead of outright permanently banning them from the game.

For years, there has been a lot of friction regarding cheating and the implementation of anti-cheat in major games like Call of Duty. Anti-cheat in gaming isn't perfect; it makes mistakes and accidentally bans people who shouldn't be banned, it can create headaches around launching the game with things like Secure Boot, and some players are placed in ambiguous "limited matchmaking" pools, a.k.a. shadow banned.

There has been a lot of mystery over how anti-cheat works, so IGN spoke with Call of Duty's senior director of game security, David Andrews, to learn a bit more about its Ricochet anti-cheat. In our exclusive interview, I asked why Activision opts to shadow ban players suspected of cheating rather than simply outright banning them there and then.

"We have limited matchmaking that we will put a suspicious account into to isolate them while other checks are either running or we're waiting on other data," said Andrews. "We're kind of doing this review process of looking at that account more holistically and seeing what's really going on here. It's kind of this stopgap measure to immediately remove them without making it be permanent [or without creating] irrevocable impact to that account and to that player, giving us some breathing room to figure out what is going on with this account and then either restoring them to the player population because it was kind of a false alarm situation."

Andrews went on to note that Activision has a variety of ways to deal with suspected cheaters, but uses techniques such as shadow banning to potentially rehabilitate a player and allow them the chance to keep playing without issue.

"We have also done some rehabilitation through the limited matchmaking saying, 'Hey, you can't do that behavior that you've just been engaged in and you can come back if you stop,' or whatever. We have a lot of enforcement capabilities. We have limited matchmaking, we have ranked play bans, we've got remote play bans, we've got temporary and permanent account suspensions, we've got hardware bans. We can do all kinds of things, and each time we're dealing with a particular style or type of cheating, we're sort of evaluating which one of these kind of makes sense for this group of cheaters. Can they be rehabilitated? Are we ultimately 100% confident in this? Is more research required? Whatever the case might be, we'll figure out what to do that's appropriate."

Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 drops next month and Infinity Ward aims to be receptive to player feedback . Anti-cheat is a big part of the optics of a Call of Duty game, and the team tested Ricochet's MW4 implementation during the recent beta. It did result in an accidental ban of a former pro player, but Call of Duty's comms team rectified the issue and confirmed it was a mistake.

Call of Duty has a reputation for cheating, especially with the free-to-download battle royale Warzone. Activision has spent a significant amount of time, money, and energy in response, even taking on cheat makers in court, although it, like all video game developers, faces an uphill battle in the war on cheaters.

Cade Onder is a freelancer for IGN's news team. He covers all things entertainment, including gaming, film, and more. You can find him on Twitter @Cade_Onder.

articles.title: Wardogs Is Coming to Xbox and PS5, but It Will Be a While
articles.summary: Wardogs, a new all-out warfare FPS game that has been blowing up on Steam, is officially coming to consoles... but it will be a while.
articles.body:
Wardogs , a new all-out warfare FPS game that has been blowing up on Steam, is officially coming to consoles... but it'll be a while.

As part of its launch, the team behind Wardogs, Bulkhead, confirmed that it will bring the massive shooter to consoles. The game is slated to arrive on Xbox and PS5 in 2028, but is available in early access on Steam starting today. The game is launching for $39.99, with plans to increase the price as the game expands. The idea is to reward fans who support the game in its earliest stages and not charge them a full $60–$70 for an unfinished product.

“Wardogs is ambitious, rough around the edges and still has a long way to go, but that is exactly what Early Access should be,” said Joe Brammer, CEO at Bulkhead. “We’re putting the game in players’ hands, listening to what they tell us and taking the risks needed to turn it into something that can last. More than anything, we want people to get online, talk to each other and have the kind of fun in an FPS that we grew up having.”

All of this suggests that Wardogs might be targeting 2028 for its 1.0 release, as PlayStation is extremely selective about early access titles on its platform, unlike Xbox. Major titles like Subnautica 2 have had to skip PS5 during early access, but there have been exceptions. However, I wouldn't hold my breath for Wardogs being one of those exceptions at the moment.

It's also interesting that Bulkhead specifically confirmed PS5 as a release platform, since PlayStation 6 is heavily speculated to release next year. Whether the game will also have a native PS6 version remains to be seen, but would presumably be playable on the next-gen console with backward compatibility should that be a supported feature.

Wardogs is one of the most surprising titles of 2026, as it really only emerged over the summer as marketing began to ramp up. However, the response from players who participated in playtests has been glowing and indicates the shooter space may have another big contender going forward.

Cade Onder is a freelancer for IGN's news team. He covers all things entertainment, including gaming, film, and more. You can find him on Twitter @Cade_Onder.

articles.title: The Original Shrek Movie Is Getting a 4K Steelbook for Its 25th Anniversary
articles.body:
Shrek is more than just a movie at this point, it's a cultural phenomenon. Ever since the first film was released back in 2001, our world has been subtly influenced by the existence of this lovable green ogre and his fairy-tale friends. We're at the point now that you can even buy a Shrek toaster that burns an image of Shrek on your toast. If that isn't a sign of late-stage Shrekitalism, I don't know what is.

While there have been several Shrek movies since the first (with a fifth movie on the way!), the original film has held up surprisingly well. The first Shrek movie is so easy to watch again and again, and watching all of the films at once is arguably one of the best movie marathons one can have. So it's no surprise that a 25th anniversary re-release of Shrek in 4K is already quite popular in the Blu-ray community.

Shrek 25th Anniversary Steelbook Is Up for Preorder, Out November 3

Shrek - 25th Anniversary Limited Edition 4K Steelbook

This isn't the first time Shrek has been released in 4K, and it won't likely be the last. The previous release was back in 2021 when the movie was first remastered for its 20th anniversary. And based on the product description, the main difference between that version and the 25th anniversary version is the cover. So if you're a collector of steelbooks, this is absolutely worth checking out, but if you already have Shrek in 4K you can probably skip.

As for what bonuses are actually included on these discs, it's actually quite a lot of extra content. There are deleted scenes, specials, commentary, and even full episodes of Puss and Boots. If you don't already own this movie, it's worth it for all of the extras alone. Some of these weren't even included in the previous 4K release.

Speaking of Shrek collectibles, DreamWorks has recently teamed up with LEGO to release some very popular new builds of everyone's favorite ogre. The first two shrek sets were released back in June and included a gorgeous 18+ build of Shrek, Donkey, and Puss and Boots . More recently LEGO has released 12 minifigures of fan-favorite characters from the series, only available via mystery boxes.

articles.title: If The World Suffered an Apocalypse Tomorrow The Global Currency Would Be Pokémon Cards, Collector and Venture Capitalist Claims
articles.summary: Pokémon cards will likely be used as currency following a global apocalypse, one venture capitalist has suggested.
articles.body:
Pokémon cards will likely be used as currency following a global apocalypse, one venture capitalist has suggested.

Pete Levin, founder of VC firm Griffin Gaming Partners, said that the "global phenomenon" of Pokémon trading cards was perfect for use as a new form of currency, should the world's current economy collapse due to some terrible catastrophe.

Levin claims to manage more than $1.6 billion of gaming assets and, handily, also happens to be the owner of some 500,000 trading cards. Speaking to The Hollywood Reporter , he explained that Pokémon cards remained a hugely profitable asset for collectors — and suggested that their worth would also be kept, at least to some degree, even after the nukes fall.

Pokémon TCG: 30th Anniversary Celebration Collection First Look

"Pokémon is a global phenomenon," Levin said. "I'm absolutely convinced that if the world suffered an apocalypse tomorrow, the following day the global currency would be Pokémon cards.

"Pokémon cards are beating the S&P 500 by 3,000%," he continued. "Emanating from Japan, it really took hold around the world in the late '90s and early 2000s. It then had a zenith moment and then a nadir moment, and ever since then, it's been on a parabolic growth curve. And that really has driven the international market expansion for trading cards."

Despite being poised to personally profit if we all started to use Charizards instead of loose change, Levin also pointed to a few other reasons he was confident in his prophecy.

For one, card grading companies such as PSA now standardize card quality ratings and provide proof of authenticity. With these, cards have a clearly quantifiable value — even if the price attached to that is left for the market to decide. Then there's the so-called "kidult" phenomenon, where adults now make up around 30% of global toy sales — a figure that's on the rise.

"You've got a generation that has come of age that is nostalgic for these toys, for these vintage video games, for these trading cards and comic books, and they now have disposable income," Levin concluded. "So that's also been a huge tangible driver in the market."

So, never mind the claim that there's a greater than 10% chance AI will end civilization in the next 10 years . If you've got a couple of Pikachu Illustrators in your back pocket, you may still be able to buy a few tins of beans.

Word that we should all begin hoarding Pokémon cards for use after the apocalypse will likely not help ongoing issues with Pokémon card scarcity, which has prompted U.S. retailer Target to begin slicing open boxes to deter scalpers . In Japan, some releases are being limited to Japanese residents only , while facial recognition for adults and children has been rolled out in some locations to limit daily card purchases .

Pokémon cards have become a prime target for scalpers and thieves over the past few years due to their soaring popularity and the perceived value of rare cards. New card releases frequently sell out completely, and The Pokémon Company has appeared unable or unwilling to fully keep up with demand — despite a staggering 10 billion cards printed last year alone .

Looking to start your collection? We've also got a list of the 10 most expensive Pokémon cards of 2026 so far , and a first look at Mega Evolution's Delta Reign expansion , set to release in November this year.
